title: Basic trie
description: A trie stores strings by shared prefixes: each node is a character, each root-to-leaf path is a string. Insertion and lookup are O(length), independent of how many strings are stored — a million words cost the same per lookup as a hundred. Autocomplete is a trie superpower: walk to the prefix node, then enumerate its subtree.
mechanism: Nodes map char -> child; terminal flag marks complete words. Prefix walk: follow characters; if any step is missing, no completions. Subtree DFS collects completions.
algo: O(L) insert/lookup for length L. Subtree enumeration is O(completions * avg length).

title: Radix (compact Patricia) trie
description: A radix trie compresses chains of single-child nodes into labeled edges, so 'vector' and 'version' share one 've' edge instead of two nodes. Memory drops dramatically for natural-language dictionaries where long shared stems are common. The trade is more complex insertion — edges split when a new word diverges mid-edge.
mechanism: Edges carry strings, not chars. Insert: walk edges matching the longest common prefix; on partial match, split the edge at the divergence point into shared prefix + two suffixes.
algo: O(L) ops with smaller constants on memory; edge splits are O(edge length). Node count drops toward the number of branch points.

title: DAWG (directed acyclic word graph)
description: A DAWG merges identical subtrees of a trie into a minimal DAG — 'taper' and 'paper' share their 'aper' tail. For a large word list it uses far less memory than a trie while keeping O(L) lookup. The price is construction complexity (minimization) and no easy deletion; DAWGs suit static dictionaries like spellcheck word lists.
mechanism: Build a trie, then minimize bottom-up: merge states with identical (transitions, terminal) signatures. Lookup walks the DAG like a trie.
algo: O(L) lookup. Minimization is O(states) with hashing of state signatures. Deletion requires rebuild.

title: FST for autocomplete
description: Finite-state transducers take DAWG minimization further: they map each string to an output value (like a popularity rank) in the same minimal automaton. Lucene's suggesters store millions of suggestions with weights in a few megabytes and enumerate completions in weight order. The FST is built offline and memory-mapped at query time — lookups never allocate.
mechanism: Compile sorted (term, weight) pairs into a minimal sequential transducer; outputs accumulate along transitions. Completion: walk to the prefix state, then traverse in an order guided by output values to emit top-weighted suggestions first.
algo: O(prefix length) to reach the state; enumeration is O(completions) with weight-ordered traversal.

title: Ranked suggestions
description: Raw prefix matches are not enough — 'a' matches a million strings, and users see five. Ranking blends static popularity (global frequency), personal history (your past picks), and context (what you typed before). The ranker runs on the candidate set only, so it can afford real features: recency decay, typo tolerance, and per-user boosts computed at request time.
mechanism: score = w1*popularity + w2*personal + w3*context + w4*match_quality. Precompute popularity; fetch personal/context features per request; sort candidates (usually < 1000) and truncate.
algo: O(candidates log candidates) sort; feature fetch is O(1) per candidate with precomputed tables.

title: Popularity weighting
description: Popularity weighting orders completions by how often each was chosen, mined from query logs. Counts are smoothed (add-one or Bayesian priors) so new suggestions are not frozen at zero, and decayed over time so last year's fad fades. The weights live in the FST outputs or a side table, updated by an offline job — never on the request path.
mechanism: weight(term) = log(1 + selections) with time decay; recompute daily from logs; bake into the suggester build. Cold-start with editorial or frequency-based priors.
algo: O(log entries) daily batch job. Query-time cost is zero — weights are precomputed.
demo:
import math, time

# selections with timestamps; weight = decayed log count
NOW = 100
selections = {'vector': [(90, 5), (95, 3)], 'vectors': [(10, 50)]}  # (day, count)

def weight(term):
    total = 0.0
    for day, cnt in selections.get(term, []):
        total += cnt * (0.9 ** (NOW - day))  # exponential decay
    return math.log1p(total)

print('vector : weight %.2f (recent picks)' % weight('vector'))
print('vectors: weight %.2f (many picks, but 90 days stale -> decayed)' % weight('vectors'))

title: Typo-tolerant completion
description: Users mistype prefixes constantly — 'vectro' should still complete 'vector'. Typo-tolerant completion walks the trie allowing k edits (Levenshtein automaton intersected with the trie), collecting candidates within budget. The walk prunes aggressively: a branch dies the moment its minimum possible edits exceed k. With k=1-2 it stays fast enough for keystroke latency.
mechanism: DFS over trie nodes carrying (prefix matched, edits used); at each node, try match/substitute/insert/delete transitions within budget. Collect terminal words reached; rank by (edits, popularity).
algo: Visits O(branching^k * prefix) nodes worst case; pruning keeps k=1 practical at keystroke speed.

title: Prefix caching
description: Autocomplete fires a request per keystroke, but prefixes nest: completions for 'vect' are a subset filter of completions for 'vec'. Prefix caching stores results per prefix and derives longer prefixes by filtering the parent's cached list — most keystrokes never touch the index. Cache entries are tiny (top-10 lists) and TTLs short, since popularity weights update daily.
mechanism: On query for prefix p: find the longest cached proper prefix q of p; filter q's cached completions by startswith(p); store. Only cache-miss prefixes hit the trie. Invalidate on suggester rebuild.
algo: Filtering is O(parent completions). Hit rate approaches 1 - 1/avg_prefix_length for steady typists.
demo:
cache, index_hits = {}, [0]
ALL = ['vector', 'vectors', 'version', 'vertex', 'vicarious']

def complete(prefix):
    # longest cached proper prefix
    for i in range(len(prefix) - 1, 0, -1):
        q = prefix[:i]
        if q in cache:
            res = [w for w in cache[q] if w.startswith(prefix)]
            cache[prefix] = res
            return res, 'derived from "%s"' % q
    index_hits[0] += 1
    res = [w for w in ALL if w.startswith(prefix)]
    cache[prefix] = res
    return res, 'index lookup'

for p in ['v', 've', 'vec', 'vect']:
    res, how = complete(p)
    print('%-6s -> %d completions (%s)' % (p, len(res), how))
print('index lookups for 4 keystrokes:', index_hits[0])

title: Incremental trie updates
description: Suggestion indexes change — new products, new names — and rebuilding a million-entry FST per change is wasteful. Incremental designs layer a small mutable delta trie over the frozen base: lookups check the delta first, then the base. A background job periodically merges the delta into a fresh base build. Deletes go in a tombstone set consulted before returning base results.
mechanism: Delta trie (mutable) + base FST (frozen) + tombstones. Insert -> delta; delete -> tombstone; lookup merges both, minus tombstoned. Merge job rebuilds base when delta exceeds X% of base.
algo: Lookup is O(L) in both structures. Merge is O(base + delta) offline — same as a rebuild but amortized.

title: Memory-efficient tries
description: A naive Python-dict trie burns ~100 bytes per node — a million-word dictionary needs gigabytes. Production tries use arrays: double-array tries (base/check), LOUDS bitvectors, or sorted child arrays with binary search. The double-array trie stores the whole structure in two int arrays with O(1) transitions and near-minimal memory; it is the standard for embedded dictionaries.
mechanism: Double-array: base[s] + code(c) = next state t iff check[t] == s. LOUDS: level-order unary degree sequence as a bitvector with rank/select for navigation. Both are built offline and read-only at query time.
algo: O(1) transition per character. Memory: a few bytes per state vs ~100 for pointer tries.
complexity: O(1) per char; bytes per state
demo:
# sorted-array children: binary search instead of dict per node (memory-slim)
import bisect

children = {}  # node_id -> sorted list of (char, child_id); words end with '#'
nodes = [[]]  # node 0 (the '#' end-marker is inserted as an edge, like any char)

def insert(word):
    node = 0
    for ch in word + '#':
        kids = nodes[node]
        chars = [c for c, _ in kids]
        i = bisect.bisect_left(chars, ch)
        if i < len(kids) and kids[i][0] == ch:
            node = kids[i][1]
        else:
            nodes.append([])
            kids.insert(i, (ch, len(nodes) - 1))
            node = len(nodes) - 1

for w in ['vector', 'version']:
    insert(w)
print('nodes:', len(nodes), '(array children, no per-node dict overhead)')
print('child chars at root:', [c for c, _ in nodes[0]])

title: Unicode tries
description: Tries over unicode must decide the alphabet: code points, UTF-8 bytes, or grapheme clusters. UTF-8 byte tries share structure across scripts for free and sort in byte order (which matches code-point order); code-point tries are simpler to reason about. Either way, normalize (NFC) before insert and lookup, or equivalent strings take different paths.
mechanism: Normalize to NFC; encode to UTF-8 bytes; build the trie over bytes. Byte order preserves code-point order, so range operations still work. Case-insensitive tries fold before encoding.
algo: O(bytes) per op. Byte tries use up to 4x the depth of code-point tries for astral characters — still O(1) per byte.

title: Mining query logs for suggestions
description: The best suggestion source is the query log: what users actually typed, in order. Session mining extracts prefix -> completed-query pairs ('vec' -> 'vector database'), filters bots and singletons, and weights by session success (did the user click something?). This beats dictionary-based suggestions because it learns the vocabulary users really use, misspellings included.
mechanism: Parse sessions into (prefix, final_query, clicked) triples; aggregate counts; drop bot patterns (inhuman rates, no clicks); weight by click-through; feed the top pairs into the suggester build as weighted entries.
algo: O(log lines) batch job. Bot filtering by rate heuristics; privacy via k-anonymity thresholds (drop pairs under K users).

title: Personalized completion
description: Personalization re-ranks completions with the user's own history: the tables you query, the files you open, the contacts you message. It runs as a client-side re-rank over the server's candidate list, so no personal data leaves the device. The features are simple — recency, frequency, and context (current project, time of day) — but the perceived quality jump is huge because the top suggestion is usually yours.
mechanism: Server returns top-N candidates with base scores; client applies personal boost = f(recency, frequency, context match) and re-sorts. Personal model stored on-device, updated from local interaction logs.
algo: O(N log N) client re-rank over N ~ 50. On-device model keeps latency and privacy both good.
demo:
import time

server_cands = ['vector', 'vectors', 'version']  # base order by global popularity
history = {'vectors': (95, 12)}  # term -> (last_used_day, uses); now = day 100
NOW = 100

def boost(term):
    if term not in history:
        return 0
    last, uses = history[term]
    return uses * (0.9 ** (NOW - last))

ranked = sorted(server_cands, key=lambda t: boost(t), reverse=True)
print('server order :', server_cands)
print('your history :', history)
print('personalized :', ranked, '(your frequent pick jumps to top)')

title: Latency targets for typeahead
description: Typeahead has the strictest latency budget in search: every keystroke should answer in under 50ms, ideally under 20ms, or typing feels laggy. The budget forces the architecture — in-memory FST, prefix caches, no per-keystroke disk I/O, and debounced requests (wait 100-150ms of typing pause). Measure p99 per keystroke position: the first character ('v') is the expensive one; longer prefixes are cache hits.
mechanism: Debounce input; serve from memory; cap candidate enumeration (top 100 by weight, then truncate to 10). Load-shed: on overload, serve prefix-cache hits only and skip the trie walk.
algo: O(1) cache hits dominate steady typing; only novel prefixes pay the trie walk. Debouncing cuts request volume ~3x.
demo:
import time

# simulate: cached prefixes are O(1); novel prefixes walk the trie
cache = {'v': 1, 've': 1, 'vec': 1}

def keystroke(p):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    if p in cache:
        pass  # O(1) filter of cached parent
    else:
        time.sleep(0.008)  # novel prefix: trie walk ~8ms
        cache[p] = 1
    return (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000

lats = [keystroke(p) for p in ['v', 've', 'vec', 'vect', 'vecto', 'vector']]
print('per-keystroke ms:', ['%.2f' % l for l in lats])
print('p99: only novel prefixes pay; steady typing is cache-speed')

title: Testing autocomplete
description: Autocomplete testing covers three layers: unit tests on the trie (insert/lookup/delete invariants), relevance tests on fixed query sets (is 'vector database' suggested for 'vec'?), and latency tests under load. Fuzzing with random unicode strings catches normalization bugs; A/B tests measure whether a ranking change actually increases selection rate. A suggester that is fast but suggests the wrong things fails the only metric that matters.
mechanism: Golden query set with expected top suggestions; assert rank positions in CI. Property tests: completions(prefix) all start with prefix; insert then lookup round-trips. Load test at 10x expected QPS with p99 assertions.
algo: O(golden set) per CI run. Property tests generate thousands of cases cheaply.
